h1: Planning winery equipment for a first vintage
title: Winery Equipment for a First Vintage | Craft Beer School
desc: What a new winery needs for its first harvest: reception, crush, press, tanks, temperature control, lab, cleaning and bottling, with buy, rent or share choices.
teaser: You do not need everything on day one. You need what the first vintage cannot do without.
standfirst: Equipment is the biggest early spend and the easiest place to overbuy. Here is a plan built around the first vintage: what to buy, what to rent and what to leave for later.
sections: Work from the process, not the catalogue

Walk through the wine from fruit to bottle and list each step. Grapes are received and checked, destemmed and crushed, pressed, fermented, settled, racked, stabilised, filtered if needed and bottled. Every item you buy should serve one of these steps. If you cannot name the step, you may not need the item yet.

Size the equipment for your first vintage, not the one in the five-year plan. A tank that sits empty still costs money, takes floor space and must be kept clean.

Fruit needs a clean, shaded place to land. You will want crates or bins, a scale and a way to measure sugar, usually a refractometer. A destemmer-crusher removes stems and breaks the berries. For a small first vintage, a compact machine is enough. Some reds are fermented with whole berries or part whole bunches, so ask your winemaker which style you plan.

Heat is the enemy of fresh fruit. In warm regions many wineries pick in the cool of night or early morning and move the fruit to the crush pad quickly.

A press separates juice or new wine from skins. White wine is usually pressed before fermentation. Red wine is usually pressed after fermentation on the skins. Basket presses suit small lots. Pneumatic presses are gentler and cost more.

Stainless steel tanks are the standard fermenting and storage vessel because they are easy to clean and hold no flavour. Temperature control is worth real money. White wine ferments best cool, often around 12 to 18 °C, while red ferments warmer, roughly 20 to 30 °C. Cooling jackets and a chiller keep a ferment in range on a hot day. A tank that overheats can lose aroma or stall. If budget is tight, choose fewer tanks of the right size with cooling rather than many without.

Pumps move wine gently and hoses connect everything. Buy food-grade hoses and fittings that you can sanitise easily and avoid long runs that are hard to clean. Wine should not be splashed. Oxygen at the wrong time harms white wine in particular. Inert gas such as nitrogen or carbon dioxide helps protect wine during transfers.

Label every hose and keep it off the floor. Drain valves and fittings are the places where old wine and microbes hide, so choose designs that come apart for cleaning.
The lab and the cleaning kit

A small lab is not a luxury. You need a hydrometer or refractometer, a pH meter, a way to measure acidity by titration and a way to check free sulphur dioxide. Sulphur dioxide is a standard preservative added at crush and later. These tests tell you when to pick, when fermentation ends and when wine is stable. Hygiene is the cheapest quality system, so budget for brushes, sanitiser, hot water and drains that work. See cellar hygiene in a small winery.

For a first vintage, many wineries hire a mobile bottler or use a partner's line instead of buying one. Rent first and buy when volume justifies it. Plan a cool, dark room for bottled wine. Warm storage ages wine too fast and spoils it. Indian summers can be severe. Buy glass, closures and labels in sensible lots. Ordering too early ties up cash. See why ageing ties up cash.

• Buy what you use every day: tanks, pumps, hoses and basic lab kit.
  • Rent or borrow what you use once a year: presses, mobile bottling and sometimes a destemmer.
  • Share with a neighbouring winery where the law and goodwill allow.
  • Skip filters, barrels or fancy kit until a wine proves it needs them.

Ask your winemaker for the list before you order. The person who runs the cellar should help choose its tools. If you do not yet have one, read when to hire a consultant winemaker.

Get at least two quotes for each major item and ask for references from small wineries that use the same machine. Check spare parts, service support and delivery time. A press that arrives after harvest is no use. Plan to receive and test equipment well before the fruit comes in, with a trial run using water.
faqs: What is the minimum equipment for a first vintage?
Fruit reception, a crusher, a press or a way to get juice, temperature-controlled tanks, pumps, basic lab kit and cleaning tools. Bottling can be hired.
Should I buy new or used equipment?
Used can save money if it is food-grade, clean and in good condition. Inspect it or take advice.
Do I need oak barrels at the start?
Only if your style needs them. They add cost and a need for care.
How much space do I need?
Enough to work, clean and store safely. Plan the layout around flow from fruit to bottle.
